hypothesis: This revised idea targets a balance-sheet resilience premium: firms with low leverage and strong gross profitability should outperform fragile, weak-margin firms because they are less exposed to distress and refinancing risk. bm is kept as a diagnostic rather than a driver, and the liquidity filter remains a transparent feasibility screen. The proposal stays directionally long resilient firms and short strained firms, with moderate confidence because of overlap risk with quality and distressed value.

This hypothesis tests whether firms with stronger short-term liquidity and higher profitability earn higher future cross-sectional returns because they are financially resilient and less exposed to distress. The core signal is a robust composite of cs_current_ratio and cs_roe, with bid and volume used only to preserve implementability. Rect_turn and cs_sp are kept only as diagnostics.

A cleaner quality-minus-expensiveness factor: long profitable, capital-efficient firms with reasonable valuation and stable liquidity, short weak, inefficient, expensive firms. The revision explicitly fixes the ambiguous role of ptb, limits curr_ratio to a secondary stability check, and emphasizes neutralization of sector and structural effects so the signal remains economically interpretable.

This hypothesis tests whether the market underprices firms that are actively investing in innovation but still look credible on liquidity and accounting quality. The signal is centered on cs_rd_sale, tempered by liquidity and accrual penalties and lightly confirmed by profitability, with explicit protection against turning into a distress trade.

This hypothesis ranks firms higher when sales growth is backed by operating efficiency, gross margin strength, liquidity, and low accrual pressure. The revision makes growth conditional on quality confirmation, which should reduce exposure to fragile or accounting-driven growers and improve robustness in cross-sectional testing.

This hypothesis is a clean cross-sectional quality spread. It longs profitable, low-accrual, low-leverage firms and shorts weak, accrual-heavy, high-leverage firms. The design is deliberately parsimonious and focuses on the most stable legs of the debate.

This hypothesis says aggressive asset growth is bearish only when it looks like low-quality, debt-supported expansion. The strongest short exposure should be in firms with high asset growth, weak gross margins, and high leverage, while profitable and conservatively financed growers should not be penalized. ask is only an execution screen, and ptb is optional for style diagnostics rather than a core driver.

This revised hypothesis keeps the original working-capital quality thesis but makes it more robust to industry effects and stale fundamentals. The signal is a cross-sectional quality-distress composite built around inventory efficiency and liquidity, with leverage as a soft penalty and earnings growth as modest confirmation. The design is intentionally simple, interpretable, and less likely to collapse into a pure sector or value exposure.
expressions: cs_rank(add(add(add(cs_rank(gpm), cs_rank(inv_turn)), cs_rank(quick_ratio)), add(sub(cs_rank(cs_earnings_growth), cs_rank(cs_leverage)), cs_rank(bm))))

hypothesis: A clean quality-versus-distress factor: long firms with high profitability, low accrual strain, and strong current liquidity; short the opposite, but only within a tradable universe defined by a hard dollar_volume screen. The mechanism is delayed recognition of fundamental durability and balance-sheet fragility, not a liquidity premium disguised as alpha.

This revised hypothesis is a slow-moving cross-sectional quality-efficiency strategy. The core return source is durable operating quality, captured by at_turn and gprof, with cs_earnings_growth acting as confirmation. Liquidity and leverage are used mainly to control distress and improve short-book tradability rather than as a standalone alpha leg. bm is kept as a diagnostic for unintended value exposure, not as a core driver.

This is a cleaner growth-quality cross-sectional signal: buy firms with strong earnings growth and high gross profitability per asset, while penalizing extreme valuation and controlling for size and tradability. The core thesis is underreaction to durable operating improvement, not a disguised value or size trade.

This hypothesis targets firms whose balance sheets are fragile and earnings quality is weak, especially when reported growth looks superficially good. The bet is that markets overvalue fragile growth and underprice the risk that accounting-driven improvement and balance-sheet stress will not persist. The signal is cross-sectional, directional, and implemented as a transparent composite with explicit stress, quality, and conditional growth layers, plus a tradability screen.
expressions: add(add(add(add(cs_rank(debt_at), cs_rank(neg(cs_current_ratio))), cs_rank(accrual)), cs_rank(neg(cs_earnings_growth))), mul(cs_rank(bm), cs_rank(neg(ask))))

hypothesis: This is a cross-sectional quality-and-safety signal: high profitability, strong short-term solvency, low accruals, and low leverage should outperform because durable firms are less likely to disappoint. Liquidity matters only for implementation, so dollar_volume is the primary screen and bid is a weak secondary guardrail.

This hypothesis targets mispricing in financially fragile firms. The core signal is a balance-sheet stress factor: weak quick ratio and high leverage should underperform because investors underprice funding risk until it becomes visible. Bid and low are secondary confirmation variables, and market_cap should be monitored or neutralized to avoid a hidden size effect.

Cash-backed value tests whether cheap stocks outperform only when their cheapness is supported by liquidity, cleaner accounting, and decent margins. It is a value hypothesis with explicit trap filters, designed to distinguish genuine undervaluation from distress.

This is a cross-sectional quality-distress signal built from liquidity, working-capital efficiency, and profitability. The expected premium comes from firms being less exposed to financing stress and operational disruption. capei is only a weak contextual overlay, while market_cap is used for universe control and size robustness rather than as part of the core mechanism.

This idea is a directional cross-sectional quality-and-balance-sheet factor: profitable, cash-rich, low-accrual, low-leverage firms should outperform because their earnings are more credible and their financing risk is lower. The revision makes the attribution problem explicit, keeps capei as a diagnostic rather than a core input, and uses only light filtering with robust cross-sectional normalization.

A parsimonious cross-sectional quality-plus-resilience factor: profitable firms with cash support and restrained leverage should outperform weaker balance-sheet names. The main alpha comes from durable quality, while dollar_volume is used only to keep the portfolio tradable.

This hypothesis tests whether firms with stronger cash buffers earn a cross-sectional return premium because markets underprice balance-sheet resilience. The core signal is a ranked cash_ratio factor, with gpm and cs_bm used mainly to identify regimes where the effect strengthens or weakens. Size and liquidity are treated as diagnostics and implementability checks rather than core alpha inputs.

This hypothesis is a pure quality-minus-fragility cross-sectional signal. It longs firms with strong profitability and asset efficiency, low accruals, low leverage, and a cash buffer, and shorts the opposite. The revision explicitly treats cash as an incremental resilience term, removes valuation ambiguity, and tightens the implementation and filtering logic.

This is a cross-sectional quality premium built from profitability, operational efficiency, accounting conservatism, and liquidity resilience. The signal is cleaner after dropping valuation and downweighting growth, while still allowing earnings growth to serve as a modest confirmation layer. The economic core is that durable, cash-backed, efficient firms should outperform lower-quality peers over a medium horizon.

A parsimonious quality-plus-fragility cross-sectional hypothesis: profitability and liquidity are the positive core, while accruals and asset growth are explicit fragility penalties. The main research task is to verify that the negative legs add incremental signal beyond the quality core and to control only lightly for microcap/low-price effects using bid, close, and shrout.

This revised idea is a parsimonious quality-versus-distress composite with a strict conditional role for book-to-market. The main edge is expected to come from high profitability and improving earnings combined with low leverage and low accruals, while cs_bm is allowed to help only when the firm is not obviously distressed. The revision converges the debate around softer distress controls, robust normalization, and slow implementation.
expressions: add(add(cs_rank(roa), cs_rank(cs_earnings_growth)), add(neg(cs_rank(de_ratio)), add(neg(cs_rank(accrual)), mul(cs_rank(cs_bm), neg(cs_rank(add(abs_val(de_ratio), accrual)))))))
add(add(cs_rank(roa), cs_rank(cs_earnings_growth)), add(neg(cs_rank(accrual)), add(neg(cs_rank(de_ratio)), mul(cs_rank(cs_bm), neg(cs_rank(add(abs_val(de_ratio), accrual)))))))

hypothesis: This hypothesis says that stocks with stronger balance-sheet resilience—high cash_ratio, low de_ratio, and supportive cs_roa—should outperform because they face less distress pressure and more financing flexibility. It keeps the core directional alpha but explicitly separates it from the extreme distress tail, which may behave more like event risk than ordinary mispricing.

This is the cleanest consensus idea: a parsimonious cross-sectional quality-minus-distress factor. The long side is firms with liquidity, modest leverage, and strong gross margins; the short side is fragile firms with weak liquidity, heavy leverage, and poor operating strength. Capei is no longer part of alpha and is retained only as a diagnostic. Implementation is conservative, low-turnover, and uses market_cap plus bid-close only as tradability screens.

A cleaner cross-sectional alpha is to buy firms with high operating margins, low accruals, high cash balances, and low leverage because they are more self-funded and have cleaner, more durable earnings. The revised version removes the ambiguous cs_sp input and adds clearer outlier handling, pre-specified screening, and separate testing of each sleeve before aggregation.

This hypothesis says that growth only matters when it is productive. Firms expanding assets are attractive if that expansion is backed by strong gross profitability and adequate liquidity; otherwise, growth is fragile and should be discounted. The factor is framed as a smooth quality-adjusted growth ranking with leverage as a fragility penalty and market_cap/volume used only to keep the strategy tradable.

This revised hypothesis ranks stocks by operating quality and balance-sheet resilience: high asset turnover, high operating margin, strong liquidity, and low leverage should outperform, especially when growth is supported by low accruals. It is a slow-moving directional quality signal with a mild growth-quality overlay and a soft distress penalty, designed to remain parsimonious and implementable with the available terminals.

A cross-sectional earnings-quality premium built around low accruals and high profitability, with quick_ratio as a modest confirming balance-sheet signal and bid/volume as explicit implementation controls. The core idea is that cleaner, more persistent earnings should outperform weaker, accrual-heavy earnings once the portfolio is screened for tradability.

A cross-sectional quality-growth signal with an explicit fragility penalty. Stocks with strong gross margins and sales growth should outperform when leverage is contained, while weak operators with high leverage should underperform. The economic logic is that debt reduces the equity value of growth by increasing distress and refinancing risk, so leverage is treated as a modifier of operating strength rather than a standalone factor.

This hypothesis tests whether cross-sectional returns are shaped by balance-sheet fragility and weak operating support. It keeps liquidity, leverage, profitability, and accrual quality as separable components, uses ptb only as a valuation control, and treats volume as a tradability screen. The idea is cleaner than the original mixed thesis and preserves the economic story of financing stress and fragility.

This hypothesis argues that the market misprices firms that are not just cheap, but cheap relative to strong profitability, efficient asset use, and improving earnings power. The edge should come from buying quality-enhanced value firms and avoiding leverage-heavy value traps. The signal is explicitly directional, cross-sectional, and parsimonious, with liquidity handled separately and leverage used as a penalty to preserve the economic interpretation.

A conditional R&D premium: high R&D is bullish only when backed by profitability and accounting discipline, and not overwhelmed by leverage or distress. The revised hypothesis is parsimonious, implementable, and explicit about sector-skew and value-contamination risks.

This revised signal tests whether the market rewards firms that are cheap, profitable, and operationally efficient while penalizing leverage. It is a simple quality-filtered value composite: high cs_ep is most attractive when supported by high ROCE and strong inventory turnover, and less attractive when leverage is high. The core thesis is durable cash generation with lower distress risk, not a complicated conditional trade.

This hypothesis says sales growth should only earn a premium when liquidity and operating quality support it. The revised spec is parsimonious, cross-sectional, and keeps ask as a minor implementation adjustment rather than part of the thesis.

This hypothesis tests whether cash-rich, profitable firms with lower leverage earn cross-sectional outperformance because they combine financial flexibility with durable operating quality. It is a low-turnover quality-and-resilience signal: cs_cash_at and roce are positive legs, de_ratio is a negative leg, pe_exi is only a weak context variable, and ask is used only to avoid expensive-to-trade names.

A parsimonious cross-sectional growth-quality hypothesis: buy firms that are simultaneously strong in sales growth and ROE, and short firms weak on both. The revision keeps the signal fundamental and cross-sectional, while treating liquidity, size, and valuation as diagnostics or implementation controls rather than core alpha terms.

A clean cross-sectional earnings-quality trade: long firms whose reported earnings are backed by cash and low accruals, short firms whose earnings rely on accruals and weak cash support. The core mechanism is earnings persistence versus accrual reversal, with cash-at-assets as an incremental support leg rather than a separate value or distress factor.
